Photius
fō´shĭ-ŭs
n. (Photius, c. 810–893, patriarch of Constantinople, the most learned Greek of his age, whose disputes with Rome produced the Photian schism and the formal Eastern rejection of the filioque)
Greek Photios, from phos, light — the enlightened.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Photius was a layman and imperial official raised to the patriarchate in 858 after his predecessor was deposed, which Rome refused to recognize. The quarrel that followed was about jurisdiction — who ruled the new Bulgarian church, and whether a pope could judge a patriarch — but Photius turned it into a doctrinal case by attacking the Western addition to the creed. The Latin church had come to say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; Photius answered that the clause was added without a council, that it had no warrant in the Greek text of Joh 15:26, and that it introduced two principles into the Godhead. His Mystagogy is the foundation of every Eastern argument since. On the procedural point he was right: no see may amend an ecumenical creed by itself, and the manner of the addition was a usurpation. On the doctrine he was wrong, for Scripture calls the Spirit “the Spirit of his Son” (Gal 4:6) and “the Spirit of Christ” (Rom 8:9), and the Son says in Joh 16:7, “I will send him unto you.” His Bibliotheca, which summarizes hundreds of books now lost, remains one of the great treasures of learning.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines procession, in theology, as the emanation of the Holy Spirit; and to proceed as to issue or come forth, as from a source.

PROCES'SION, n. The act of proceeding or issuing forth, as from a source.

In theology, the emanation of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.

PROCEED', v.i. To issue or come forth, as from a source.

Key Scripture

Joh 15:26 — "But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:"

Joh 16:7 — "Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you."

Gal 4:6 — "And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father."

Rom 8:9 — "But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his."

Modern Corruption

Photius was right that Rome had no authority to amend the creed alone and wrong about what the amended creed said, and the East has kept the error with the grievance.

expand to see more

Two things must be held apart. The filioque entered the Western creed by regional usage and papal sanction rather than by an ecumenical council, and that is a real fault: a creed received by the whole church is not one see's property. Photius's procedural objection deserves the concession the West has rarely made. But the doctrine itself is scriptural. The Spirit is sent by the Son (Joh 16:7), is called the Spirit of the Son (Gal 4:6) and the Spirit of Christ (Rom 8:9), and the eternal procession answers to the temporal sending. Joh 15:26 says He “proceedeth from the Father” and in the same verse that Christ will send Him; it does not exclude the Son, and the Greek argument requires it to.

The second corruption is the ecumenical trade now commonly proposed, in which the West drops the clause to purchase reunion and calls the difference a matter of emphasis. Amo 3:3 asks whether two can walk together except they be agreed, and the question of how the Persons subsist is not an emphasis. The Reformed churches confess the filioque with the whole Western tradition, and the honest path is to defend it from Scripture rather than to barter it, while granting Photius his point that no bishop may rewrite the church's confession by himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ekporeuomai (G1607), to proceed, to go forth; pempo (G3992), to send; parakletos (G3875), Comforter.

Greek pempo (G3992) — to send; John 15:26, John 16:7.

Usage

"“even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father” (Joh 15:26) — the clause he stood on."

"“but if I depart, I will send him unto you” (Joh 16:7) — the Son sending."

"“God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts” (Gal 4:6) — the Spirit called the Son's own."
